q: Name an operating system first released before 1990.
hint: Its first version shipped or went into use before January 1, 1990. Later versions are fine.

answers.l: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie started it at Bell Labs in 1969 on a spare PDP-7.
Microsoft bought 86-DOS from Seattle Computer Products in 1981 and licensed it to IBM and other PC makers.
System 1 shipped with the original Macintosh in January 1984; the last major version of the line, Mac OS 9, came out in 1999.
Gary Kildall wrote it in 1974 for Intel 8080 systems; its BIOS layer let it run on many different machines.
A joint MIT, GE and Bell Labs project begun in 1964; it went into production use at MIT in 1969.
DEC announced it with the VAX-11/780 in 1977 and shipped V1.0 in 1978; its lead Dave Cutler later led Windows NT at Microsoft.
Bill Joy's first Berkeley Software Distribution came out in 1978 as add-ons to Research Unix.
Shipped with the Amiga 1000 in 1985 and brought preemptive multitasking to a home computer.
IBM and Microsoft released OS/2 1.0 in December 1987; it was text-only until 1.1 added Presentation Manager.
Andrew Tanenbaum released it in 1987 with his textbook; Linus Torvalds used it before writing Linux.
IBM's branded version of DOS; 1.0 shipped with the IBM PC 5150 in 1981.
AT&T's commercial Unix, first released in 1983; its Release 4 merged in features from BSD and SunOS.
Microsoft's licensed version of AT&T Unix, announced in 1980 and later handed over to SCO.
IBM's operating system for System/360, announced in 1964; Fred Brooks drew The Mythical Man-Month from managing it.
Shipped with the Atari ST in 1985; its desktop was Digital Research's GEM.
Apple contracted Shepardson Microsystems to write it in 1978 for the Apple II's Disk II floppy drive.
Apple's 1983 replacement for Apple DOS on the Apple II, adding hierarchical directories and hard disk support.
Bell Labs' 1979 release, the first to include the Bourne shell and the ancestor of most later Unixes.
MIT's Compatible Time-Sharing System, first demonstrated in 1961 under Fernando Corbato.
Sun's BSD-based Unix from 1982; the name Solaris 1 was later applied to it when SVR4-based Solaris 2 arrived.
IBM's Unix, first released in 1986 for the IBM RT PC.
Hewlett-Packard's System V based Unix, first released in 1982.
SGI's Unix for MIPS workstations; the 'It's a Unix system' scene in Jurassic Park shows its 3D file browser.
NeXT released 1.0 in 1989; Tim Berners-Lee wrote the first web browser on it, and it became the basis of Mac OS X.
Gordon Bell and Dan Dodge released it as QUNIX in 1982; its microkernel now runs in many car infotainment systems.
Wind River's real-time OS, released in 1987; it ran NASA's Mars Pathfinder lander in 1997.
IBM's Multiple Virtual Storage, released in 1974; its lineage continues today as z/OS.
Digital Research's MS-DOS compatible from 1988; Windows 3.1 betas carried the AARD code that warned against it.
Tim Paterson wrote it at Seattle Computer Products in 1980; Microsoft bought it to become MS-DOS.
Berkeley Softworks brought a windowed graphical interface to the Commodore 64 in 1986.
Acorn first shipped it as Arthur in 1987 with the Archimedes, Acorn's ARM-based home computer line.
CMU microkernel begun in 1985 by Richard Rashid; it became the core of NeXTSTEP and later Apple's XNU.
IBM's integrated OS for the AS/400 from 1988, with a built-in database; it is now called IBM i.
Novell's network operating system from 1983, which dominated PC file and print sharing into the 1990s.
Released in 1975; John Lions' annotated commentary on its source became a famous photocopied text.
DEC's BSD-based Unix for VAX and later MIPS DECstations, first released in 1984.
IBM released it in 1972, giving each user a separate virtual machine, usually running CMS.
Built at IBM's Cambridge Scientific Center in the late 1960s as CP-40 and CP-67; it pioneered full virtualization.
DEC's PDP-10 operating system, first shipped in 1967 as the PDP-10 Monitor.
DEC's 1976 OS for the DECSYSTEM-20, derived from BBN's TENEX.
Written at BBN around 1969 for modified PDP-10s; Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked email from it.
MIT AI Lab's Incompatible Timesharing System, named as a jab at CTSS; Emacs began on it.
DEC's real-time PDP-11 OS from 1972; Dave Cutler led RSX-11M before VMS.
DEC's small single-user real-time OS for the PDP-11, released in 1970.
CP/M for the 8086; offered for the IBM PC in 1982 at 240 dollars against 40 dollars for PC DOS.
Tandy's disk operating system for the TRS-80 line of microcomputers.
Microware's Unix-like real-time OS, written in 1979 for the Motorola 6809; unrelated to Mac OS 9.
Ran Pascal bytecode on a virtual machine; it was one of three OSes IBM offered for the original PC.
The MSX standard's disk OS from 1984, with a file system compatible with MS-DOS.
Apple's 1983 OS for the Lisa, with protected memory and cooperative multitasking that the first Mac lacked.
Apple's 16-bit operating system for the Apple IIGS, released in 1988.
Apple's System V based Unix for 68k Macs, first released in 1988; later versions ran Mac apps alongside Unix tools.
Symbolics' Lisp machine operating system, written almost entirely in Lisp.
Edsger Dijkstra's layered OS at Eindhoven, described in 1968; it put his semaphores to practical use.
Master Control Program of the Burroughs B5000, written in the high-level language ESPOL rather than assembly.
Dartmouth's time-sharing system, launched in 1964 alongside BASIC by John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz.
IBM's smaller System/360 OS from 1966; its descendant lives on as z/VSE.
Dick Pick's database-centric OS, first built for TRW in 1965 as GIRLS.
Commodore's ROM-resident OS core for 8-bit machines like the VIC-20 and Commodore 64, called through a fixed jump table.
Disk OS for the Atari 400 and 800, released in 1979 and written by Shepardson Microsystems.
SCO's System V/386 based Unix from 1989, later renamed OpenServer.
DEC's time-sharing OS for the PDP-11, popular in schools for running BASIC-PLUS.
DEC's main operating system for the PDP-8, from 1971.
Digital Research's 1979 multi-user, multitasking version of CP/M.
Technical Systems Consultants' disk OS for Motorola 6800 and 6809 machines in the late 1970s.
The Sophisticated Operating System of the 1980 Apple III; ProDOS borrowed its file system.
Mark Williams Company's Unix clone, first released in 1980 for the PDP-11 and written without AT&T code.
Apollo's networked workstation OS, first released as Aegis in 1981.
Douglas Comer's teaching OS from Purdue; the name stands for Xinu Is Not Unix.
Per Brinch Hansen's 1969 nucleus for the Danish RC 4000, an early microkernel design.
Ran the Manchester Atlas from 1962 and managed its pioneering paged virtual memory.
Written in 1956 by General Motors and North American Aviation for the IBM 704; often called the first operating system.
GE's 1960s mainframe OS; the gecos field in Unix /etc/passwd is named after it.
Began as EXEC 8 on the UNIVAC 1108 in 1967 and is still maintained by Unisys.
University of Michigan's time-sharing OS for IBM mainframes, in use from 1967 to 1999.
IBM's time-sharing OS for the System/360 Model 67, released in 1967 and later withdrawn.
IBM's System/38 OS from 1978, whose single-level storage design OS/400 inherited.
Descends from IBM's Airline Control Program built for 1960s airline reservations; still used for bookings and card payments.
Hewlett-Packard's Multi-Programming Executive for the HP 3000 minicomputer, introduced in 1972.
Tandem's fault-tolerant OS from 1976, built for banks and exchanges that could not go down.
Prime Computer's minicomputer OS, written largely in FORTRAN and later PL/P.
Data General's 32-bit OS for the Eclipse MV line, the machine chronicled in The Soul of a New Machine.
The Machine Operating System in the BBC Micro's ROM, released in 1981.
The multitasking OS of the 1984 Sinclair QL, designed by Tony Tebby.
A portable OS written in BCPL at Cambridge in the late 1970s; it became AmigaDOS.
Niklaus Wirth and Jurg Gutknecht wrote it and its language for the Ceres workstation at ETH Zurich in the late 1980s.
An embedded real-time OS from 1982, later acquired by Wind River.
Intel's real-time multitasking OS for its own processors, first released in 1980.
Cray's Unix, first released in 1985, which replaced COS on its supercomputers.
A network OS built on Unix System V; its StreetTalk directory service predated Novell's NDS.
AT&T's Programmer's Workbench Unix of 1977, which shipped with the SCCS version control system.
AT&T's Unix release of the early 1980s from its Unix Support Group, which preceded System V.
A Unix-like real-time OS from Lynx Real-Time Systems, first released in the late 1980s.
Digital Research's multitasking successor to Concurrent CP/M, able to run several DOS programs at once.
Whitesmiths' Unix-like OS from 1979, one of the earliest Unix clones.
Xerox PARC's single-user OS written in Mesa, used on the 1981 Xerox Star.
A microkernel distributed OS from INRIA's Chorus project, begun in 1979.
A portable message-passing OS from the University of Waterloo in the 1970s.
Built by the SHARE user group for the IBM 709 around 1959.
IBM's tape-based operating system for the 7090 and 7094 in the early 1960s.
ICL's operating system family for its 1900 series mainframes.
ICL's Virtual Machine Environment for its 2900 series mainframes, developed in the 1970s.
Control Data's time-sharing OS for 6000 series machines in the early 1970s; it evolved into NOS.
Control Data's Network Operating System for its Cyber mainframes, from the 1970s.
Control Data's batch operating system for the CDC 6600 era supercomputers.
Project Genie's 1960s system for the SDS 940; Butler Lampson worked on it.
Stanford AI Lab's PDP-10 OS derived from TOPS-10; Donald Knuth developed early TeX on it.
Stratus Computer's fault-tolerant operating system, which shipped with its first systems in 1982.
Data General's Real-time Disk Operating System for the Nova minicomputer.
Siemens mainframe OS from the 1970s, still maintained by Fujitsu.
Norsk Data's operating system for its NORD and ND minicomputers.
DEC's time-sharing system for the PDP-8, released in 1968.
Hunter and Ready's real-time kernel from 1981, among the first commercial RTOSes.
Intel's disk OS for its Intellec microcomputer development systems in the 1970s.
The Software Link's multiuser DOS-compatible OS, released in 1987.
COS, Cray Research's batch operating system for the Cray-1 and X-MP.
Honeywell's 1979 OS created to move Xerox CP-V customers onto Honeywell mainframes.
Control Program Five for the SDS and Xerox Sigma mainframes, offering time-sharing in the early 1970s.
Sequent's Unix for its multiprocessor Balance and Symmetry systems.
VenturCom's real-time Unix, ported to the IBM PC and DEC Professional in the early 1980s.
Heath Company's disk OS for the Heathkit H8 and H89 microcomputers.
John Ousterhout's distributed Unix-like OS, developed at UC Berkeley from 1984 to 1992.
A microkernel distributed OS from David Cheriton's group at Stanford in the 1980s.
Tanenbaum's distributed OS at Vrije Universiteit; Guido van Rossum created Python while working on the Amoeba project at CWI.
A capability-based OS for CMU's C.mmp multiprocessor in the 1970s, from William Wulf's group.
Key Logic's capability-based OS for IBM System/370, released in 1983 and descended from GNOSIS.

nope.Windows: Windows 1.0 (1985) was a graphical environment running on MS-DOS; Windows NT, the first standalone one, shipped in 1993.
nope.Linux: Linus Torvalds released the first Linux kernel in 1991.
nope.Solaris: SVR4-based Solaris 2 shipped in 1992; Sun's earlier systems ran SunOS.
nope.Plan 9: Bell Labs' first public Plan 9 release came in 1992.
nope.Mac OS X: Mac OS X arrived in 2001; the 1984 Mac ran Classic Mac OS.
nope.GNU Hurd: The GNU project began in 1983, but Hurd development started in 1990 and it never had a pre-1990 release.
nope.FreeBSD: FreeBSD 1.0 came out in 1993; the original BSD dates to 1978.
nope.BeOS: Be Inc. first shipped BeOS in 1995.

traps.q: Which operating system's name began as a pun on Multics?
traps.l: Brian Kernighan is credited with the name Unics, a play on Multics, later spelled Unix.

traps.q: Which operating system, written by Gary Kildall in 1974, did IBM consider before choosing a DOS from Microsoft for the IBM PC?
traps.l: Talks between IBM and Digital Research stalled in 1980, and IBM licensed what became PC DOS from Microsoft instead.
